American Express stock faces revenue test after Q3 guidance boost
sum: American Express is entering its next reporting phase after raising its 2026 earnings outlook with its third-quarter results. A Yahoo Finance analysis published Wednesday, November 4 says the focus is shifting from the earnings beat to the quality of the increase and the pace of future revenue growth.

Third-quarter revenue increased 9 percent year over year to a record 20.1 billion US dollars, while adjusted earnings per share rose 13 percent to 4.68 US dollars. Billed business, a key measure of spending on the network, climbed 8 percent to 454.0 billion US dollars. The net write-off rate improved to 1.8 percent from 1.9 percent a year earlier, pointing to better credit performance during the period.

Management lifted its 2026 earnings-per-share guidance to a range of 18.30 to 18.60 US dollars from 17.30 to 17.90 US dollars. The analysis notes that the higher range includes a pretax gain of 982 million US dollars from the sale of American Express's stake in Global Business Travel Group. On an adjusted basis, the outlook is 17.60 to 17.90 US dollars after accounting for the gain and a restructuring charge.

The operating picture is stronger than the headline profit increase alone suggests, but revenue momentum has moderated. Third-quarter revenue growth slowed from 10 percent in the second quarter to 9 percent, and commercial spending increased only 3 percent, or 5 percent excluding co-brand portfolios that American Express exited.

The analysis also highlights a lower tax rate of 18.1 percent, compared with 24.1 percent a year earlier. That change contributed 0.29 US dollars per share to the quarter, making the reported earnings improvement less purely operational. For investors, the central question is whether card spending, fee income and credit quality can sustain earnings growth while customer engagement and funding costs remain elevated.

sum: American Express reported third-quarter revenue of $20.06 billion and adjusted EPS of $4.68, beating estimates and raising its full-year earnings floor. However, the profit beat relied primarily on a lower tax rate, credit reserve releases, and share buybacks rather than operational acceleration, with billed business growth slowing to 8%. Technically, the stock maintains a cautiously bullish bias above the $313.02 support level. A daily close above immediate resistance at $327.24 could trigger further upside toward $343.10.

TradingKey - American Express (NYSE: AXP) reported third-quarter results before the open on Friday, October 23, beating on adjusted EPS and raising its full-year earnings outlook. The stock closed at $325.17 on Thursday, up 0.48%, and premarket trading sits slightly lower near $323.00. Even after a gain of about 4% this week, shares are down about 12% this year.

Underneath the beat, a lower tax rate, a release of credit reserves and buybacks did most of the work, while card spending growth slowed. That is likely why a beat-and-raise has not lifted the stock before the open.

Revenue rose 9% to a record $20.06 billion, roughly in line with the $20.12 billion consensus. Adjusted EPS, which strips out one-off items, rose 13% to $4.68, above estimates of about $4.49 to $4.58. GAAP EPS jumped 31% to $5.42 and net income rose 28% to $3.71 billion. Billed business, the total amount spent on Amex cards, rose 8% to $454.0 billion.

The gap between GAAP and adjusted results comes from two items. Amex booked a $982 million pre-tax gain from selling its stake in Global Business Travel Group and took a $336 million restructuring charge tied to efficiency plans.

Amex raised its full-year GAAP EPS guidance to $18.30 to $18.60, from $17.30 to $17.90. On an adjusted basis, which excludes the travel stake gain and the restructuring charge, the new range is $17.60 to $17.90. That lifts the floor but leaves the top of the old range unchanged. Amex still expects revenue growth of about 10%.

Strip out the stake gain and the restructuring charge, and pre-tax income rose only about 1% from a year earlier. The 13% adjusted EPS growth leaned on three things. The effective tax rate fell to 18.1% from 24.1% because of discrete benefits from settling prior-period tax items.

Both American Express (NYSE:AXP) and Verizon Communications (NYSE:VZ) report Q2 2026 results before market open on Friday, July 24, 2026, with Verizon's earnings call confirmed for 8:30 AM ET. For a retirement-focused investor deciding which name to hold into the earnings report, the question is simple: which one is Wall Street actually leaning into? The setup favors two very different profiles. American Express trades at $348.74 with a 22 P/E, while Verizon trades near $44.29 at an 11 P/E. Here is how they stack up across three dimensions that matter this week.

American Express carries 14 Buy, 15 Hold, and one Sell ratings, a modest lean toward neutral with a single dissenter. Verizon's coverage skews cleaner on the downside: 11 Buy, 15 Hold, and zero Sell ratings. No sell-side analyst is telling clients to exit Verizon, and that matters for a retirement holder who cares about tail risk in the coverage universe. American Express has more outright Buys, but the presence of a Sell and a heavier Hold cluster tempers conviction.
Winner: Verizon. Zero Sell ratings versus one, with a similar Hold count, gives Verizon the cleaner buy-side floor.

American Express has an analyst consensus target of $374.94, almost 8% higher than the current price, alongside an AI model target of $391.47, implying 12.25% upside. Verizon's consensus target is $51.12, with an AI model target of $49.99, implying 12.88% upside. On percentage upside to the model target, Verizon has a hair more room. On absolute dollar distance to consensus, American Express has further to travel. What tips the scale for a retirement investor: Verizon's year-to-date price performance is already +8.7%, while American Express is −5.7% year to date. Verizon is compounding into its target; American Express needs a re-rating.

American Express (AXP) experienced significant intraday volatility and closed in negative territory on Wednesday, driven primarily by a broader market downturn linked to escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Financial markets faced a sharp sell-off globally after comments from U.S. President Donald Trump indicated that the tentative ceasefire agreement with Iran was effectively over, triggering fears of a wider and more disruptive conflict.

The abrupt breakdown in diplomatic relations immediately sent global crude oil prices surging more than five percent, which in turn stoked investor anxieties regarding renewed inflationary pressures and the potential for a tighter monetary policy environment from the Federal Reserve. This escalation sparked a pronounced risk-off shift among institutional and retail investors. Large-cap financial stocks and payment processors, including American Express, are highly sensitive to macroeconomic shifts, as geopolitical instability and rising energy costs pose a threat to discretionary consumer spending, travel activity, and overall transaction volumes.

Furthermore, American Express is uniquely exposed to travel and premium lifestyle spending. The spike in energy prices heavily weighed on the travel sector, pulling down airline and cruise lines due to fears of rising operational costs. Because a significant portion of American Express's revenue is tied to high-end travel, hospitality, and corporate entertainment, the sudden downturn in the travel ecosystem added downward pressure on its stock price.

On the micro-level, today marked the official implementation date for American Express's tighter Centurion Lounge access rules. These rules now require guests to be booked on the same flight itinerary as the primary cardholder and cap connecting layover visits at five hours.
